title.narrative: Improved national capacity to develop sustainable enterprises for inclusive economic growth, decent jobs and just transition

description.narrative: Bangladesh’s economic growth relies on micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), which account for 25% of GDP and nearly 90% of employment. However, most operate informally, facing low productivity, limited access to finance, inadequate business services, and weak integration into national and global value chains. This results in working poverty, low wages, and vulnerable livelihoods, especially among women, youth, and marginalized groups. The expected loss of preferential trade benefits following Bangladesh’s Least Developed Country (LDC) graduation by 2026 heightens the urgency to formalize enterprises and enhance competitiveness, productivity, and value addition across key sectors. ILO’s strategy focuses on fostering responsible, inclusive, sustainable, and green economic development by supporting entrepreneurship, MSME formalization, value chain development, and responsible business practices. ILO aims to provide technical support to the Ministry of Industry and SME Foundation on policy formulation, social dialogue, and capacity building. Target sectors include tourism, ICT, agriculture, and care services, for their potential to create decent jobs and promote entrepreneurship. Expected results include strengthened national and sectoral policies for MSME growth and formalization, access to tailored business development services, adoption of responsible business practices, and improved sectoral productivity. The strategy aims to create new and higher-quality jobs, while supporting Bangladesh’s just transition to a green economy. Beneficiaries are women, youth, persons with disabilities, CMSMEs, and vulnerable host communities and Rohingya refugees in Cox’s Bazar. Partners include national ministries (Industry, Education, Youth & Sports), agencies such as SME Foundation, Bangladesh Investment Development Authority, and Bangladesh Bank, as well as employers’ organizations, chambers of commerce, development banks, and UN agencies.
